tagline: Personal finance dashboard for budgeting, transactions, goals, and net worth.
verdictSummary: A CSV-first finance dashboard — import bank exports, categorize with simple rules, track budgets and net worth — is a real weekend build, and it keeps bank credentials out of the picture entirely. What doesn't come with it is live bank and investment sync, which needs a data-aggregation service most personal projects shouldn't try to build themselves.
coreLoopDIY: Import bank and card CSV exports, categorize transactions with simple rules, track budgets and account balances, and chart net worth over time.
whatYouLose: transaction categorization tuned by a maintained service
whyPeopleStillPay: Personal finance apps are only valuable when the data arrives automatically and safely — people pay so linking a bank account isn't something they build and secure themselves.
notes: A good kinda: the spreadsheet-replacement half is a clean yes, live bank sync is genuinely harder.
prompt:
Build a CSV-first personal finance dashboard: import bank and card CSV exports, with a per-bank column mapping saved after the first import and rows deduped by a date-amount-description hash so re-imports are always safe. Categorize with simple rules — a substring or pattern match on the description sets the category automatically — and give a fast review screen for whatever's left uncategorized. Track monthly budget targets per category with actual-versus-budget bars, and a manual-entry accounts table (for things without CSVs, like a pension or property) feeding a net-worth chart built from balance snapshots you enter periodically. Add a recurring-charge detector: the same merchant at a similar amount on a roughly monthly cadence gets flagged and listed with its annualized cost — this subscription-audit view alone often justifies the build.

Do not build automatic bank sync, multi-user household accounts, or mobile apps — no bank credentials should ever need to enter this system, and the monthly CSV import ritual is the honest price of keeping it that way.

faq.q: Can I import my existing Monarch Money data?
faq.a: Monarch lets you export transactions to CSV, and that maps directly onto this build's import flow. Investment holdings and net-worth history generally don't export cleanly, since those come from Monarch's own data aggregation.

faq.q: Will it work on my phone?
faq.a: As a responsive web page, yes, for viewing and quick entry. There's no dedicated app and no automatic bank sync, so checking in requires more deliberate effort than a five-second phone glance.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Hosting and a database, typically a few dollars a month — genuinely inexpensive since this handles no live bank connections.

faq.q: What's the one thing that doesn't survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Automatic sync. Every number here arrives through a manual CSV import, which means the dashboard is only ever as current as your last import — a real behavior change from data that updates itself.
